target: Infrastructure / distributed systems / platform / SRE internships, 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table into a Redis-cached category tree to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits, which became the Claude skill’s main search tool
bullet_feedback.problem: The reason clause 'to keep lookups within the database’s permission and rate limits' is ambiguous: 'permission limits' is not a standard capacity concept, so an infra reader can't tell whether the constraint was read QPS, row-level access control, or both. The tail 'which became the Claude skill’s main search tool' then switches the subject to the AI feature, so the caching decision (the infra-relevant part) ends without a mechanism-level outcome.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most capacity-flavored bullet in the Capital One block; if the constraint reads as vague, the reader files it as 'added a cache' rather than 'designed around a rate-limited datastore'.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'permission limits' means here (access-scoped queries vs. a query quota), and what 'popular' was based on.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the constraint concretely first (e.g., the shared table's per-client query limit), then the precompute-and-cache design, then that it became the skill's main search path. Drop 'permission' if it isn't a throughput constraint.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-built a research tool that scores and aggregates topics to show Amazon Leo’s public-policy staff what’s popular, which runs in dev on AWS Fargate with GitHub Actions CI/CD and AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code ready for production
bullet_feedback.problem: The second half is a deployment-stack list (Fargate, GitHub Actions, CDK) with no decision or result attached, and 'runs in dev ... ready for production' tells the reader it isn't in production. 'Co-built' plus 'scores and aggregates topics' leaves the candidate's own piece undefined.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For platform/SRE readers, IaC and CI/CD are only interesting when tied to what they enabled (repeatable environments, gated deploys); as written it reads as name-dropping and is the weakest of the three Amazon Leo bullets.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which part the candidate owned (the CDK stack? the pipeline? the scoring service?) and what the CDK/CI setup bought (e.g., one-command environment creation, deploy gating).
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the infra piece the candidate personally owned and what the IaC/CI setup made possible; shorten the product description to a short clause. Keep the honest 'in dev' scoping.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut end-to-end latency 34% on a data pipeline that sends 6,000+ scraped research documents to model inference by streaming them through Amazon Kinesis into AWS Lambda instead of staging each step in S3
bullet_feedback.problem: Strong mechanism-plus-result, but the 34% has no absolute baseline or unit (per-document latency? batch completion time for 6,000 docs?).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Interviewers on streaming teams will immediately ask whether this is p50 per record or wall-clock for the batch; the answer changes how impressive it is.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what latency was measured (per-document vs. whole run) and, if known, the before/after values.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add a two-to-three-word qualifier on what latency means (e.g., 'per-document' or 'batch'); no other change needed.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio’s class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
bullet_feedback.problem: Ends at intent ('to reduce database load and latency') with no observed effect, and the only number (20,000+ visits) describes the product's traffic, not the cache.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can't tell whether the cache mattered at that load; 20,000 visits over 30 days is low QPS, so without a result an infra interviewer may wonder why caching was needed.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what was cached (which queries, invalidation approach) and any observed effect on DB load or response time.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name what the cache was keyed on or how it was invalidated, which adds depth without a new metric; if an observed effect exists, state it instead of the intent clause.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the engine’s event log to compare them on identical 2M-record workloads, which showed the B+ tree giving 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries for 27% more disk
bullet_feedback.problem: Only the read side of the tradeoff is reported. The classic reason to pick an LSM-tree is write throughput, so a storage-engine reader will notice that write performance is missing from the comparison.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the most storage-engine-specific bullet on the page; a one-sided comparison invites the 'what about writes?' question and slightly weakens the tradeoff framing.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: how the two backends compared on write/ingest throughput, if that was measured.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: If write numbers exist, swap one read figure for the write result so the bullet shows both sides; otherwise leave as is.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting a Claude skill into focused sub-skills that call Python search and validation tools instead of searching open-ended
bullet_feedback.problem: 'instead of searching open-ended' is a compressed phrase that a non-ML reader won't parse, and 'Claude skill' / 'sub-skills' is product-specific jargon.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor: the 65% and 'under 15s' carry the bullet, but the contrast clause is what explains the mechanism.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase the tail as a plain contrast, e.g. 'instead of letting the model search freely'.

page_feedback.problem: The strongest infra/performance evidence on the page (the IEX order book: 50.9M-message replay, 1.26M events/sec, B+ tree vs LSM-tree comparison) sits in Projects at the bottom, below four experience blocks, three of which are mostly AI-tooling or app work.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A 7-second skim for an infra/SRE role sees AWS + Capital One AI workflow bullets first; the throughput, storage-engine and correctness numbers an infra HM hires on are found only if they read to the end.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Consider moving Projects above the shorter UMIACS/TerpLabs entries, or above Experience entirely for infra-targeted versions; AWS can stay first.

page_feedback.problem: The AWS bullet (EC2 capacity bounds for Redshift patching, availability vs. cost) is the single most domain-relevant line, but it is the only bullet under the most recognizable brand and uses present-progressive 'Writing', which reads as in-progress task description.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Capacity-vs-availability tradeoffs are exactly what this domain screens for; the bullet is good but a reader may skim past it as a placeholder.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the content; consider an active present-tense verb ('Build'/'Designing') and front-loading 'capacity planning for Redshift patching' so the domain keyword lands first.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists services that never appear in any bullet (API Gateway, SNS, X-Ray, OpenSearch, SQLAlchemy).
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Not a problem on its own, but an infra interviewer may probe one of these and find thinner experience than implied.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only items the candidate can discuss in depth, or be ready to back each one up.

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine to replay 50.9M real IEX exchange messages without ever resyncing, which agreed with the exchange on 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices

Writing backtested Java capacity-planning logic that sets upper and lower bounds on the EC2 capacity Amazon Redshift reserves for patching to balance availability against cost

Built an EventBridge-scheduled LLM-as-judge check for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance to trigger fine-tuning only when its grades shift past a threshold
Cut research-environment setup time 30% by pinning dependencies with uv and packaging the environment in Docker so every machine gets an identical setup
Section structure, single-column layout, and right-aligned dates/locations
